title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (4 of 7)
hook: the third quarter: deep sleep, where you want nothing and dream nothing
tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: the second quarter, taijasa, the shining one. The dream, lit from within. Did you notice the world light up as you fell asleep? Day two hundred fifty-six.

Here's a strange thing everyone says. I slept so well last night. How do you know? You weren't there. There was no you, no world, no dream, nothing to remember. And yet you wake up and report it, with total confidence, as the best part of your night. Something was present enough to enjoy it. The Mandukya's third quarter is that deep, dreamless sleep. And the way it describes it is almost tender.
screen: `I SLEPT SO WELL.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW?` → `THE THIRD QUARTER.`

segments.voice: Verse five: where the sleeper desires no desire and sees no dream, that is deep sleep, sushupta. The third quarter is prajna, the knowing one. Its field is deep sleep. It has become one; it's a single mass of knowing. It is made of bliss, anandamaya, and it enjoys bliss. Its mouth is consciousness. Stop on those words. A mass of knowing, not a knower of things. In waking you know the world; in dream you know images. In deep sleep there are no objects at all, so the knowing isn't split up among them. It's gathered, like light with nothing to fall on. And it's made of bliss: that's why you wake up and say, I slept well. No wanting, no fear, no problems. Commentators notice something else: in deep sleep, the poor person and the king are exactly equal. Then verse six says something even larger about this third quarter: it is the lord of all, the knower of all, the inner controller, the source of all; the beginning and the end of beings. Why? Because the waking world and the dream world both come out of deep sleep every morning and fold back into it every night. It's the seed they grow from. And the sound: m, the lips closing. The hum at the end of om, where the sound gathers before it stops. So now you have three: waking and a, dreaming and u, deep sleep and m. Tomorrow, what the Mandukya calls simply the fourth.
screen: `NO DESIRE, NO DREAM.` · `PRAJNA: A MASS OF KNOWING.` · `MADE OF BLISS.` · `THE SOURCE AND THE END.` · then, large: `THE THIRD QUARTER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Let the body get heavy, as if you were drifting toward sleep, but stay just awake. Let go of wanting anything from these two minutes. Let go of any images. If thoughts come, let them pass without following. See if you can taste a little of what the text describes: no wanting, nothing to hold, just a quiet, gathered knowing. Don't try to fall asleep. Just rest near it. The bell holds the time.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The third quarter is prajna: deep sleep, no desire, no dream, a single mass of knowing, made of bliss.
Your line: the fourth. Tomorrow morning, when you wake, ask what it was that slept so well. Day two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often use the everyday report 'I slept well' as a starting point for reflecting on deep sleep as the Mandukya's third quarter, prajna.

fork.setup: you wake up and say 'I slept so well.' but you weren't aware of anything. how does the Mandukya explain it?
options: deep sleep is a mass of knowing, made of bliss.
fork.reveal: prajna, the third quarter: no desire, no dream, knowing gathered into one, enjoying bliss.

original.note: Sanskrit: sushupta, deep sleep, fast asleep; Mandukya 5: the field of prajna.

trapdoor: what you thought: in deep sleep, you're just switched off.
what it means: the Mandukya calls it a gathered knowing, made of bliss, the seed of waking and dream.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya 5 calls prajna ekibhuta, prajnanaghana, anandamaya and cetomukha; 6 calls it the yoni, womb, of all.
